entries.title: The two dequeue idioms are one three-way rendezvous
entries.text: The links orders:dequeue ⊗ workers:acquire and orders:dequeue ⊗ payment:do:reserve are binary, but they share the dequeue port, and Flatten's union-find merges their classes into one: fused:orders/dequeue+payment/do_reserve+workers/acquire, a single flat transition that fires orders/dequeue, payment/do_reserve and workers/acquire as one. That is what licenses the spider-fusion drawing: two event spiders that share a leg fuse into one spider with three legs, because fusion is computed over equivalence classes, not pairwise (compose_fuse.go:9-20, unionfind.go). So the three idioms leave two event classes, not three; the other is fused:payment/commit+workers/release. The ROADMAP sketch draws one sync spider per idiom, and after fusion two remain. How it was established: tests/gopflow.test.mjs compares the page's Flatten with go-pflow's FlattenWithMap on 11 configurations (fused groups, wires, the place and transition maps), and tools/chyp/flatten-crosscheck.mjs runs it on both link orders and on a cycle: dequeue~acquire then dequeue~do:reserve, and the reverse order, both give the one three-member class (10 transitions); dequeue~acquire alone gives fused:orders/dequeue+workers/acquire (11); the default links, in either order, give the two classes above (9 transitions).

entries.title: go-pflow's capacity check is post-firing and net of what the firing consumes
entries.text: go-pflow's capacity check (firing.go:129-194) is a post-firing bound, applied only to the places a firing raises and net of what that firing consumes there: a transition is refused for capacity only if, after it fires, a place it raises would hold more than its capacity. A place already over its bound does not block a firing that leaves it alone or lowers it. That happens: fusing places sums their initial markings but keeps the tighter capacity (compose_flatten.go:291-292), so the pool-share configuration (workers:available token-linked to workers2:available, a second pool of capacity 1) starts with 3 tokens on wire:workers/available against a capacity of 1, with no warning; go-pflow's receipt shows an empty warnings list and both acquire transitions enabled at the initial marking. The first JS port of the firing rule was stricter, and the cross-check against go-pflow's own EnabledWhyNot caught it (tests/gopflow.test.mjs compares the reason for every flat transition at the initial marking, on every configuration that flattens, pool-share included). This is about the engine, not about the default composition: the bounded places here are the queue's items and slots (capacity 3) and the pool's available and in_use (capacity 2).

entries.title: The orders composition is not a lens composite
entries.text: queue ⊗ pool ⊗ saga, as go-pflow composes it, is not a lens composite. A lens composite needs a boundary to compose along, a backward map in every part, and the parts' backward maps to fire together the way their forward maps do. (1) No boundary is glued: among orders, workers and payment go-pflow allows 0 token and 0 data links (72 event and 66 guard), because the three patterns' place schemas all differ (cq/13 predicted it, and go-pflow agrees), and the composition uses 0 place links, so the composite is ⊗ plus transition fusion. Event fusion is a rendezvous, not a composition along a boundary. (2) Every part does have a backward map, found mechanically (a residual place only t produces and only u consumes, and u returns what t moved on resource places): do_reserve → undo_reserve and do_charge → undo_charge in the saga, acquire ⇄ release in the pool, enqueue ⇄ dequeue in the queue. Only the saga's are compensations; the pool's and the queue's are plain inverses. (3) The backward maps do not fire together. Going forward, dequeue, do_reserve and acquire fire as one, but their backward maps enqueue and undo_reserve fire as separate transitions, and the pool's release is fused into the forward commit, so the way back has nothing to fire it. Only do_charge / undo_charge composes, inside the saga. The forward pass is taken from the commit scenario (judgment, frozen). The runs agree: refund and charge-fails end with workers/available = 1, expected 2, and go-pflow's own run gives the same markings. How it was established: the test is computed from go-pflow's link rules and its Flatten as the page ports them, never from a reading; both ports are cross-checked against go-pflow (tests/gopflow.test.mjs), and tests/lensfind.test.mjs pins the pairs, the legal-link counts and the split first step.

entries.title: No single link makes the orders composition a lens composite
entries.text: The pool has one release. Fusing it with undo_reserve as well as commit (adding workers:release ⊗ payment:undo:reserve) makes one transition, fused:payment/commit+payment/undo_reserve+workers/release, that needs both committing and unwind_reserve, and saga_control keeps exactly one token among the saga's control places, so it can never fire and every scenario deadlocks: commit stops at payment/commit, refund and charge-fails at payment/undo_reserve. Moving the link instead (dropping release ⊗ commit and adding release ⊗ undo_reserve) fixes the refund (the worker returns, workers/available = 2) and leaks on commit (workers/available = 1). The third repair tried, adding orders:enqueue ⊗ payment:undo:reserve, joins the queue's backward map to the saga's and leaves the refund leaking. No repair makes the strict test hold. An event link only adds a rendezvous (all members fire as one); a lens needs the pool released on either outcome, which is a choice no link kind expresses (the idiom's own caveat: releasing on both outcomes is not expressible with the declared ports). How it was established: each repair is validated by go-pflow's rules, flattened, analysed again, and the scenarios re-run (lensfind.tryFixes); go-pflow c802f34 (tools/gocheck with the two wirings as extra configs) gives the same runs and stopping points, as recorded in the prototype's commit message for the lens view, not in a receipt.

entries.title: Spivak's wiring diagrams are undirected cospans
entries.text: Spivak's operad of wiring diagrams (arXiv:1305.0297, Ex. 2.1.7) is undirected: a wiring diagram is a cospan of ports onto cables, with no inputs or outputs, and filling a hole is a pushout of cable sets. A directed version appears there only in §6.3 (Future work), as the subject of a paper then in preparation. The operad view's reviewer corrected an earlier note that said wiring diagrams wire outputs to inputs. So an event link is drawn as an undirected junction (⊗) on one cable, not as a wire from an output to an input: it is a synchronisation (Bruni et al.), as in the cospan operad of Fong-Spivak §6.5 (Ex. 6.94), whose wiring diagrams have ports but no left and right. Here the three event links make two junctions, one per fused class, and the dequeue ⊗ acquire ⊗ do:reserve junction has three legs. The in / out sides drawn are go-pflow port kinds, kept for reading; the operad does not see them.

entries.title: Chyp proves event-link fusion independent of link order, on the orders example
entries.text: sync-spiders.chyp reads an event link between two transition handles as the spider m ; n, and a connected set of links as one spider. The 10 rules it assumes are a special commutative Frobenius algebra, read from compose_fuse.go:9-20; Chyp's own checker, headless, proved all 12 rewrites built only from them (12 of 12, including frobL and frobR from Chyp's examples/frobenius.chyp). On the orders example: L1 (dequeue ~ acquire) then L2 (dequeue ~ do:reserve) is the one three-member class; L2 then L1 is the same class, so the order of the two links does not matter, and the same holds on the member transitions orders_dequeue, workers_acquire and payment_do_reserve; where L3 (release ~ commit) sits in the link list does not matter either; a~b then b~c equals b~c then a~b; a cycle a→b, b→a is one class; a link given twice is one link. The page's port of Flatten computes the same classes on both link orders and on a cycle (tools/chyp/flatten-crosscheck.mjs; see the three-way rendezvous finding). Not equational, so not modelled: naming (Link.ID refusing two links that name one class differently), arcs (a fused transition's arcs are merged by sum), guard links, and token and data links. Chyp checks that each rewrite follows from the stated rules; it does not check the rules, which are a person's reading of compose_fuse.go and are marked ASSUMED. sync-spiders.chyp is untyped on purpose, every wire being a Sync handle, because typed identities fail to compose at Chyp 3d28483. As a check on the checker, a mutation run over the four theory files changed one step's term in 36 mutants and that step failed every time.

entries.title: In Chyp at 3d28483 a bare rewrite step never checks
entries.text: A bare rewrite step (Chyp's refl) never checks at 3d28483, even a ; id = a. This is upstream behaviour, diagnosed from the code: Tactic.run for refl returns validate_goal() != None (tactic/__init__.py:99-100), and validate_goal only looks for an isomorphism (proofstate.py:263-270), so it never pops the goal; checker.check marks a step VALID only when the goal count drops (checker.py:99-104). A direct test on Chyp's examples/smc.chyp gave refl.run() = True with goals 1 → 1 for all 20 bare steps, and find_iso found an isomorphism for each. The GUI calls the same checker.check (gui/editor.py:349), so it should show these steps red too; that was not observed, because the GUI was not run. For the laws here this means the theory files contain no bare steps. The one purely symmetric-monoidal fact needed, L3_position_irrelevant (where the release ~ commit link sits in the link list), is closed by simp() with no rules: simp ends in the same isomorphism test but pops the goal (tactic/simptac.py:53-63), and the control NOT_simp_not_iso shows that simp() still refuses a pair that is not isomorphic.

entries.title: Chyp at 3d28483 has no rewriting modulo Frobenius
entries.text: Chyp implements the rewriting of monogamous acyclic hypergraphs (its README, line 11) and cannot rewrite on graphs where one vertex has several producers or consumers: the double-pushout rewrite raises 'Rewriting modulo Frobenius not yet supported.' (rewrite.py:51, 53). Event fan-out and spider fusion are exactly that case. So in sync-spiders.chyp the spiders are explicit generators (m, u, n, v) with the Frobenius rules as assumed rules, and each fusion of the orders example's event links is an explicit chain of single steps; comm and cocomm match every m and n, so simp would loop on them and they are used only as single steps. Chyp also has no nested boxes (which is why the search plan's drivers are drawn as Search → Search boxes after the core) and no one-way rules ('<=' is refused: 'Non-invertible rules currently not supported', state.py:272-273), so nothing about order relations is checked.
